context: material-handling led (dry bulk) or tank/piping led (liquid bulk) · marine civil is the enabler

brief.intro: New to this project type? A bulk terminal moves cargo that is not packed in containers — either dry bulk (coal, ore, grain) or liquid bulk (fuel, chemicals) — between a ship and onshore storage. Dry bulk terminals are built around a conveyor chain: stacker/reclaimer, transfer towers and a ship-loader or unloader moving material to and from stockpiles. Liquid bulk terminals are built around a tank farm connected to the jetty by process piping, pumps and loading arms. Both share the same marine civil (jetty or quay) and the same instrumentation/SCADA-led control philosophy, but the equipment that actually moves the product — not the marine structure — is what drives the schedule.

scope.name: Marine civil
scope.desc: Jetty or quay construction and the berth the vessel moors against.

scope.name: Stockyard / tank farm civil
scope.desc: Stacking pads and drainage for dry bulk, or tank foundations and bunding for liquid bulk.

scope.name: Conveyor trestle / pipe rack
scope.desc: The structural supports carrying conveyors or the pipe rack between jetty and shore facilities.

scope.name: Material handling equipment (dry bulk)
scope.desc: Conveyors, stacker/reclaimer and ship-loader/unloader that move bulk material.

scope.name: Tank farm & process piping (liquid bulk)
scope.desc: Storage tanks, pipeline, pumps and loading arms that transfer liquid product.

scope.name: Electrical power
scope.desc: Substations and motor control centres (MCCs) driving conveyors, pumps and equipment.

scope.name: Instrumentation & SCADA
scope.desc: Weightometers, level and flow instrumentation, and the control system operators run the terminal from.

scope.name: Dust suppression / fire & safety
scope.desc: Dust extraction and explosion venting for dry bulk, or fire-foam and vapour recovery for liquid bulk.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Conveyor/stacker run-in and interlock proving, or pump/loading-arm and pipeline testing.

glossary.plain: the machine that piles bulk material into a stockpile and later reclaims it onto a conveyor.
the crane-like machine that loads or unloads bulk cargo directly to or from the ship.
the structure where one conveyor hands material to the next, changing direction.
a belt scale that measures material flow rate for stock control.
a containment wall built around tanks to hold a spill.
the articulated pipe connecting the jetty pipeline to a tanker for liquid transfer.
safety systems that prevent or vent a dust explosion in enclosed handling areas such as grain or coal.
the control system operators use to run and monitor the whole terminal remotely.

must_get_right: The material-handling chain (conveyors/stacker-reclaimer, or pumps/piping) is the schedule driver, not the marine jetty — sequence its procurement first.
Dry bulk needs dust-explosion protection proven before any load-out trial; liquid bulk needs pipeline hydrotest and fire-foam proven before product is introduced — do not skip either to save time.
The marine civil (jetty/berth) and the conveyor trestle or pipe rack must be coordinated early — the structural interface is fixed once piled.
SCADA and weightometer or flow-meter calibration are commercial (custody transfer) measurements — leave real time for calibration and acceptance, not just a functional test.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are tied to the equipment train or berth section; the network is calculated (F9) with total float kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Marine civil works are weather and tide dependent; equipment erection runs a standard 6-day week; commissioning moves to a 7-day calendar to cover the load-out trial window, which is usually tied to a real vessel call.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs marine civil/trestle or tank-farm civil → material-handling equipment or tank/piping erection → electrical & instrumentation → dust/fire protection proving → load-out trial. In dry-bulk mode the driver is conveyor/stacker-reclaimer procurement and belt commissioning; in liquid-bulk mode it is tank hydrotest and pipeline reinstatement — name the applicable one explicitly.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and a single mobilisation is assumed; the berth or jetty is available to the equipment-erection schedule as planned; and product introduction (first cargo) is scheduled against a confirmed vessel call, not an assumed date.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is procurement-led — the following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Storage tanks — shop or field-erected (liquid bulk)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Marine plant access is tide and weather dependent; heavy-lift windows are needed for the stacker/reclaimer or large tanks; dust- or hazardous-area works require permits and specialist crews; the final load-out trial is constrained by vessel-call scheduling.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: equipment delivery slippage, dust-explosion or fire-system re-test loops, tank hydrotest/settlement time, and vessel-call availability for the trial. Schedule contingency is held immediately before commissioning and before the load-out trial rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for equipment erection and commissioning — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
